clue.text: Hard worker and I soundly passed old Italian course

indicators.note: soundly means going by how the word passed sounds when spoken, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: the ant is the proverbial hard worker
taken as written, joined on by and
past is pronounced the same as passed
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A diligent labourer and the speaker skipped an outdated dish at an Italian meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian course' looks like it might be a lesson in the language; it is a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasto is the starter served before the main dishes of a traditional meal in Italy.

clue.text: 23 with clothes on — could be more beautiful topless?

indicators.note: without its top, the word loses its first letter, which sits at the top of a down entry

blocks.note: fair means beautiful, so more beautiful is fairer

explanation.surface: A daring joke: someone dressed up might look better without a top on.
explanation.walkthrough: 23 is HORSE, so the definition is a clothes horse, a frame for drying laundry. Dropping the first letter of FAIRER leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An airer is a folding frame on which washing is hung to dry, commonly called a clothes horse.

clue.text: Irritable if constrained to give evidence

indicators.note: constrained means held in, so the short word is held inside the longer one

blocks.note: testy is a synonym for irritable
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grumpy witness, held back by conditions, is made to speak in court.
explanation.definitionFit: To testify is to make a statement under oath, as a witness does before a court.

clue.text: Rich man with animated dog wrecked cart

indicators.note: something wrecked is smashed up, so the letters of cart are broken and rebuilt

blocks.note: Pluto is the Disney cartoon dog
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A wealthy man's lively dog has smashed up a cart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Animated' suggests a lively dog, but it means a cartoon one.
explanation.definitionFit: A plutocrat is a person whose power or status comes from great wealth.

clue.text: Bound, completely, to do house work

blocks.note: to bound is to leap, or spring
clean can mean completely, as in clean forgot

explanation.surface: Someone is wholly obliged to get on with the household chores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' reads as obliged, but it is a leap.
explanation.definitionFit: To spring-clean is to give a home a thorough top-to-bottom tidying, traditionally each year after winter.

clue.text: Unacceptable excuse

blocks.note: first meaning: not allowed
second meaning: a way of escaping an obligation

explanation.surface: A lame excuse is dismissed as not good enough.
explanation.definitionFit: Something forbidden is said to be out; an escape route or alibi is also called an out.

clue.text: Music left by the Savoyard in boat

indicators.note: left by means abandoned by, so those letters are dropped from the music

blocks.note: skiffle is 1950s folk-jazz music played on homemade instruments
Savoy is a French-speaking region, and the French for the is le

explanation.surface: A tune is left behind on a boat by a performer of Gilbert and Sullivan.
explanation.walkthrough: A Savoyard usually means a Gilbert and Sullivan performer (they played at the Savoy Theatre); here it is someone from Savoy who speaks French.
explanation.definitionFit: A skiff is a small light rowing or sailing vessel.

clue.text: Energetic steps taken to involve a doctor in special appeal

indicators.note: to involve is to draw in, so the outer pair of letters takes the others inside

blocks.note: SA is short for sex appeal; special stands for its S
taken as written
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: Lively action is needed to bring a physician into a special plea.
explanation.walkthrough: SA for sex appeal is a crossword convention; here 'special' stands in for sex, a joke on the surface sense of appeal.
explanation.definitionFit: The samba is a lively Brazilian dance, so its moves are energetic steps.

clue.text: Complaint made by one taking learners to head

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
L is a learner, from the L-plates on British learner drivers' cars; two of them make LL
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: Someone moaned when a single instructor brought trainee drivers to the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' is a grievance on the surface, but a medical complaint is meant; 'taking' and 'to' just string the parts together.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in the medical sense is an ailment or disorder of the body.

clue.text: Anticipation of a setter providing anagram for it

indicators.note: the setter openly says the words supply a jumbled version of the answer

blocks.note: all nine letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A compiler has a sneak preview of what the solver will face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' does double duty: it reads as part of the definition but its letters are part of the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A foretaste is an advance sample or early experience of something still to come.

clue.text: He may make dramatic savings in his deliveries

definitions.text: He may make dramatic savings in his deliveries

blocks.clueFragment: He may make dramatic savings in his deliveries
blocks.note: surface reading: a thrifty person, perhaps a delivery man or a bowler, who cuts costs spectacularly
setter's reading: saving lives dramatically by delivering people from danger

explanation.surface: A tradesman manages to cut his delivery costs remarkably.
explanation.walkthrough: Saving and delivering both mean freeing someone from danger.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who pulls people out of danger saves and delivers them, often dramatically.

clue.text: Pigeon's an acrobatic performer

blocks.note: first meaning: a breed of domestic pigeon that somersaults in flight
second meaning: a gymnast who does somersaults and handsprings

explanation.surface: A bird is described as a showy circus act.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the pigeon breed and the gymnast take the name from rolling over and over through the air.

clue.text: Thick-skinned type briefly supplying money

blocks.note: first meaning: the short form of rhinoceros, an animal with a famously thick hide
second meaning: old British slang for cash

explanation.surface: An insensitive person quickly hands over funds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thick-skinned type' sounds like an unfeeling person; it is the animal. Rhino as slang for money is old-fashioned British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a clipped name for the armoured-looking animal and also dated slang for cash.

clue.text: Seller of publications, including novel and learned books

blocks.note: novel means new
sage as an adjective means wise or learned
NT, the New Testament, is a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A bookseller stocks fiction alongside scholarly volumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' and 'books' sound like the shop's stock, but they give the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A newsagent is a shopkeeper selling newspapers and magazines, which are publications.

clue.text: Outside, one's immersed in river, for certain

indicators.note: something immersed is sunk inside, so the letter for one goes inside the river

blocks.note: without is an old word for outside, as in within and without
the Fal is a river in Cornwall
I is one, and the 's means is

explanation.surface: Someone outdoors has definitely gone for a dip in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fal is a short river in Cornwall, south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Without fail means invariably or definitely, so it can replace for certain in a sentence.

clue.text: Secular song

blocks.note: first meaning: not of the clergy
second meaning: a short narrative poem or ballad

explanation.surface: A song that is not religious.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay describes people outside the clergy, and is also an old word for a ballad or poem to be sung.

clue.text: Member arrives unpunctually to pass laws

blocks.note: a limb is a member of the body
read as is, as in he is here
unpunctual means late

explanation.surface: A parliamentarian turns up behind time for a vote on new laws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a member of parliament, fitting the surface; it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a parliament's job is enacting statutes, which is exactly what this verb describes.

clue.text: It's clear it's arranged for public performers

indicators.note: arranged means put into a new order, so the letters are set out afresh

blocks.note: all eleven letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone states plainly that something has been organised for entertainers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' fits music too, which helps the surface hide its job.
explanation.definitionFit: Recitalists are musicians or reciters who give recitals, which are performances before an audience.

clue.text: Weariness of Northern girl embracing endless study

indicators.note: endless here means losing both ends, the first and last letters
embracing means hugging, so the girl's word wraps around the other piece

blocks.note: lassie is a Scottish and northern English word for a girl
taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: A girl from the north is worn out from studying without end.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassitude is a state of physical or mental tiredness and lack of energy.

clue.text: Some of our betters do it and are ruined

definitions.text: Some of our betters do it

blocks.clueFragment: Some of our betters do it
blocks.note: first meaning: gamblers (betters) go to greyhound racing, the dogs
second meaning: an idiom for falling into decline

explanation.surface: A grumble that some of the upper classes have fallen into ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our betters' reads as social superiors, but it means people who bet; in Britain 'the dogs' is greyhound racing.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to the dogs is a common idiom for deteriorating badly or falling to ruin.

clue.text: It's an idea, albeit daft in the extreme

indicators.note: the extreme of a word is its far end, so only the last letter of daft is kept

blocks.note: albeit means though
the final letter of daft

explanation.surface: Someone concedes a suggestion is worth having, even if it is utterly silly.
explanation.definitionFit: A thought is a notion or idea produced by thinking.

clue.text: It sounds like the main responsibility of a bishop

indicators.note: sounds like says the answer is pronounced as the next word, though spelt differently

blocks.note: the main is a poetic name for the ocean, and that word is pronounced the same as the answer

explanation.surface: A remark on a bishop's chief duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main' looks like an adjective, main responsibility, but the main is the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: A see is the diocese or area over which a bishop has authority.

clue.text: Racket made by farm animals around Donegal's borders

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the animals wrap the letters taken from the county
the borders of a word are its outermost letters, first and last

blocks.note: swine are pigs
the first and last letters of Donegal

explanation.surface: Pigs on an Irish farm are making a terrible din.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket' sounds like noise, which farm animals make, but it means a scam. Donegal is a county in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a dishonest scheme for getting money, which is a fraud or con.

clue.text: Material line in 1982 film

blocks.note: a line of goods is a stock carried by a shop
taken as written
E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial was released in 1982

explanation.surface: A piece of fabric, or a line of dialogue, appears in a 1982 movie.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockinet is an elastic knitted fabric, the kind of textile used for underwear and bandages.

clue.text: Ringing sound a Dickensian shop-girl heard

indicators.note: heard means the answer is what the listener catches by ear rather than reads

blocks.note: Little Nell is the heroine of Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop; the answer's K is silent

explanation.surface: Someone hears a bell ring in a shop from a Dickens novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A knell is the slow tolling of a bell, especially for a death or funeral.

clue.text: Language pupil's environment hard to take

blocks.note: the iris is the coloured ring surrounding the pupil of the eye
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A schoolchild finds a foreign tongue difficult to learn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pupil' and 'Language' paint a school scene, but the pupil is in the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Irish is the Celtic language of Ireland, also called Gaelic.

clue.text: Copenhagen, for example, included in author's excursion

indicators.note: included in says the answer is already contained in the next words, running across them

blocks.note: the letters run from inside author's into excursion

explanation.surface: A writer travels to the Danish capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Copenhagen was the Duke of Wellington's horse at Waterloo, not just the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Copenhagen is the name of a famous mount, so it is an example of the animal.

clue.text: Reinforce American investigators in a disheartened unit

indicators.note: disheartened means losing the heart, so the middle letters of the word go
in places the investigators inside what is left of the other word

blocks.note: taken as written
G-men are FBI agents in American slang
taken as written before its middle goes

explanation.surface: US detectives are sent in to strengthen a demoralised squad.
explanation.walkthrough: G-men (government men) is 1930s American slang for FBI agents.
explanation.definitionFit: To augment is to increase or add to something, which strengthens or reinforces it.

clue.text: Flap when striker is knocked over

indicators.note: something knocked over is turned upside down, which in a down entry flips the order of letters

blocks.note: a bat is used to strike the ball

explanation.surface: Panic breaks out when a batsman or footballer is felled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flap' looks like panic and 'striker' a footballer, but the striker is a bat.
explanation.definitionFit: A tab is a small flap or strip attached to something, used to pull or label it.

clue.text: In pieces, and sure to be replaced

indicators.note: replaced means put back in a different position, so the letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: all seven letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something broken is bound to need replacing.
explanation.definitionFit: Asunder means apart or into separate parts, as in torn asunder.

clue.text: Praise for taking one pound off former charge

indicators.note: taking off removes something, here a single letter standing for a pound

blocks.note: ex means former
a toll is a charge for using a road or bridge

explanation.surface: A cheer goes up for knocking a pound off a fee that used to be charged.
explanation.walkthrough: L is the standard abbreviation for pound, from the Latin libra.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to praise someone or something highly and enthusiastically.

clue.text: Thought that is abandoned before arriving at summerhouse

indicators.note: abandoned means left behind, so those two letters drop out

blocks.note: thought, as a past tense, means believed
i.e. stands for id est, Latin for that is
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: An idea is dropped just before someone reaches a garden pavilion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thought' looks like the definition but is the word that loses IE.
explanation.definitionFit: A belvedere is a summerhouse or turret built to command a fine view.
